blocks.text: Yet there follows something far more παραδοξότερον [paradoxoteron], namely that the chicks, hatched in this way by a foreign mother, leave her some time later in order to return to their true mother, whom they recognize by her voice. Eustathius, in the place cited above: Αὐξηθέντες οἱ νεοττοὶ, [II, 639] ἕκαστος, κατὰ γένος, πρὸς τοὺς οἰκείους ἀνίπταται, καὶ ἔρημόν αὐτὴν καταλιμπάνουσι· [Auxēthentes hoi neottoi, hekastos, kata genos, pros tous oikeious aniptatai, kai erēmon autēn kataleimpanousi] When the chicks have grown up, each one, according to its kind, flies back to its own parents, and they leave her alone. Ambrose, in the Hexaëmeron: When she has brought out her chicks, she loses them; for when they have heard the voice of the one who produced the eggs, they leave her and betake themselves, by a kind of natural love and duty, to the one whom they have recognized as their true mother by the generation of the eggs, showing that this one performs the office of a nurse, that one of a parent. And in the Letter to Sabinus: When all the labour spent on nourishment has exhausted the one rearing them, and the chicks have begun to grow up, then she (the true mother) utters her voice, and calls her offspring with a kind of trumpet of devotion. The offspring, roused by a kind of natural hearing, recognizes its parent and deserts the pretender. Thus, when she wishes to gather what she did not bear, she loses those whom she thought to rear. Philastrius: and when the time of discerning age has grown upon them, then, having let go (read dimissis [having dismissed]) their false parents, remembering by their own sense the rights of parents, and seeing them openly with their eyes, they no longer delay to follow them. Cassiodorus: But as soon as the young have begun to have confidence in walking, they go out into the fields with their nurse; and once they have been prompted by the maternal voice, they seek rather the mother of their eggs, although they are reared by others as stolen offspring. Isidore: When the chicks have heard the voice of their own mother, by a kind of natural instinct they leave the one who brooded them, and return to the one who bore them. Damir: في طبع الحجل ان ياتي اعشاش نظاريه فياخذ بيضها فيحضنه فانا اطارت الفراخ لحقت بامهاتها التي باضتها [fī ṭabʿ al-ḥajal an yaʾtī aʿshāsh naẓārīh fa-yaʾkhudh bayḍahā fa-yaḥḍunuh fa-anā aṭārat al-firākh laḥiqat bi-ummahātihā allatī bāḍat-hā] It is of the nature of the partridge that it comes to the nests of birds similar to itself, takes their eggs, and broods them; but the chicks, when they fly off, attach themselves to their mothers who laid them. Porta coeli: והביצים ההם כשיבקעו ויצאו האפרוחים לא יהיו כמו בניו שילכו אחריו אלא יעזבוהו ולא יכירוהו ולא ילכו אלא אחרי מי שהוא להם, But after the eggs are hatched and the chicks have come forth, they do not behave as its chicks, so as to follow it; rather they desert it, and no longer know it, nor do they follow any other except the true mother. For שהוא להם read שהוא להם אם, as in Kimchi, who has these same things on Jeremiah. The reader sees that by these writers something scarcely credible is asserted: namely, that partridge chicks know by nature from which mother came the egg out of which they were hatched, and that they at once recognize her by her voice, though they have never before heard or seen her. Who would believe that such a sense belongs to egg-laying creatures rather than to viviparous ones, which generate more perfectly? Or that brutes excel in it rather than man, who, it is perfectly plain, has no natural knowledge of his parents? Otherwise Oedipus would not have unwittingly killed his father, nor lain with his mother. Accordingly, in the Poet, Telemachus, asked whether he was the son of Ulysses, answered thus ^{a)}:

[II, 640] Μήτηρ μέν τ᾽ ἐμέ φησι τοῦ ἔμμεναι αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε Οὐκ οἶδ᾽. οὐ γάρ πώ τις ἑὸν γόνον αὐτὸς ἀνέγνω. [Mētēr men t' eme phēsi tou emmenai autar egōge ouk oid'. ou gar pō tis heon gonon autos anegnō.] [col. 86]
My mother indeed asserts that I am his; but I do not know. For no one has ever himself known his own begetter. And Menander, quoted by Eustathius on that passage:
Αὑτὸν γὰρ οὐδεὶς οἶδε τοῦ ποτ᾽ ἐγένετο, ᾽Αλλ᾽ ὑπονοοῦμεν πάντες, ἢ πιστεύομεν. [Hauton gar oudeis oide tou pot' egeneto, all' hyponooumen pantes, ē pisteuomen.]

No one knows of himself by whom he was begotten; we all suspect, or believe. And even if what they relate of partridge chicks were true, it could still hardly, if at all, have been observed. For suppose that, of the many chicks following a mother partridge, one or two desert her to go to another: who would dare to affirm for certain that this happens because they were hatched from eggs stolen from that other bird? How many things must be presupposed for this observation to be held true and established? And so nothing of the kind occurs among the ancient writers on natural history. Jerome's memory deceived him when he wrote on Jeremiah: The writers of natural history, of beasts and birds as well as of trees and plants, the chief of whom among the Greeks are Aristotle and Theophrastus, and among us Pliny Secundus, say that this is the nature of the partridge: that it steals the eggs of another partridge, that is, another's eggs, and sits on them and broods them; and when the brood has grown up, it flies away from it and leaves the foreign parent. But the pious men too who, with him, committed this fiction to writing placed more faith than was fitting τοῖς τερατολόγοις [tois teratologois], whose aim was to hold the people's attention with these prodigies of storytelling. For, as Synesius rightly says in the Encomium of Baldness, Τὸ δὲ ῥᾷστον καταγελάσεται ὁ δῆμος· δεῖται γὰρ τερατείας. [To de rhaston katagelasetai ho dēmos; deitai gar terateias.] What is easy, the common people laugh at; for it craves marvellous narration.
